newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US pledges to boost Rwanda genocide tribunal.
newsitem.headline: US pledges to boost Rwanda genocide tribunal.

text.p: The United States offered its full support on Thursday for the war crimes tribunal investigating Rwanda's genocide.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck and Richard Bogosian, Bill Clinton's envoy for Africa's Great Lakes region, said Washington would give diplomatic and financial support to help the U.N. tribunal bring the killers to justice.
"Justice must be done as speedily as possible. We'd expect the pace of trials to increase. The tribunal now is on a very strong path," said Shattuck.
Added Bogosian: "This tribunal is relatively young. Inevitably it has taken some considerable effort to get it under way. It has a very difficult task."
They were speaking at a joint news conference following a two-day Geneva meeting with donor countries under Washington's auspices to discuss ways of speeding up the tribunal's work.

Since its creation in November 1995, the tribunal has indicted 21 genocide suspects of whom 13 are in custody. But key organisers of the Hutu-led slaughter of more than half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates in 1994 remain at large.

Shattuck said his government would send an expert team to Rwanda for witness protection, a major concern, and give $500,000 to help finance Rwandan radio coverage of trials at the tribunal seat in the Tanzanian town of Arusha.
More than 100,000 Hutus accused of genocide are stuffed into overcrowded jails in Rwanda, where many Tutsi survivors want an eye for an eye after one of this century's worst mass killings.

The genocide raises some of the most intractable questions of administering justice in a country where thousands of people killed under duress, crowds surrounded churches where massacres were happening, parents were forced to kill their enfants and even seven-year-olds admitted to killing.

Rwanda's paralysed justice system, trying to come to terms with complex genocide crimes, has started its own trials for suspects and sentenced 32 people to death out of 52 defendants tried since late 1996.
